detailed_rationale:
Wipro's Q1 FY27 (quarter ended June 30, 2026) print confirms the pattern that has defined this stock for several years: record deal bookings that have not yet translated into organic growth. IT services revenue of $2.61bn was up just 0.9% YoY in constant currency but DOWN 1.2% sequentially, and management guided Q2 FY27 to a range of -1.5% to +0.5% cc — i.e., still flat-to-negative at the midpoint. This follows a FY26 in which full-year IT services dollar revenue actually fell 0.3% YoY. Large-deal TCV was genuinely strong — $1.63bn in Q1 (+12.9% QoQ, 13 deals) on top of a record FY26 of $16.4bn (+14% YoY) — but Wipro has a multi-year history of touting large-deal momentum that ramps slower than peers' equivalent pipelines, and this quarter's revenue print is the latest data point in that pattern rather than a break from it. Segment mix is a genuine concern: Americas 1 and Americas 2 (60.6% of revenue combined) both declined sequentially (-2.3%/-2.5%), and Energy/Manufacturing/Resources fell 8.9% YoY, while only Europe (+6% YoY) and APMEA (+13.5% YoY) — smaller books — grew. IT services margin came in at 16.0%, down 130bps sequentially and roughly 120bps YoY, on wage hikes, large-deal ramp costs and AI investment; layered on top is the industry-wide H-1B $100k fee (effective since Sept-2025) that analysts size at a 50-150bps margin headwind, though Wipro's H-1B book (1,523 visas per FY25 filings) is smaller than TCS's (5,505) or Infosys's (2,004), giving it modestly less relative exposure than the two largest peers. [DATA]

On capital allocation, Wipro executed and completed its Rs 15,000 crore buyback in mid-June 2026 and declared a further Rs 2/share interim dividend, taking cumulative shareholder returns (dividends + buybacks) past $3bn over the trailing year — a genuinely shareholder-friendly and well-funded (98% OCF/NI conversion, D/E 0.23, interest coverage 12.2x) capital return programme. But this is now a completed, one-time event rather than a forward catalyst. Leadership churn continues to be a live risk during a period when execution matters most: Americas2 CEO Suzanne Dann resigned this year, the CTO departed, and the company is mid-reorganization — splitting HR leadership (a dedicated CHRO for the new AI-Native Business unit) and bringing in an ex-Accenture executive (Amit Kumar) to run Wipro Consulting/Capco, which reports directly to CEO Srini Pallia. These moves could eventually fix Capco's chronic consulting drag, but as of this print there is no delivered evidence yet — only new hires and reorganized reporting lines. Attrition ticked up to 13.9% and there was zero fresher onboarding in Q1, both consistent with a company managing costs defensively rather than gearing up for growth. [DATA]

On valuation: Wipro trades at ~14.1-14.2x trailing earnings, essentially in line with TCS (~14.8x) and Infosys (~14.5x) and at a discount to HCLTech (~18.3x), against a sector average near 19x. A ~14x multiple on a mature, high-payout IT services business implies the market is pricing in only a modest (mid-single-digit, roughly 5%) forward growth bar — not a demanding one. The problem is that Wipro has not cleared even that modest bar organically for two straight fiscal years (FY26 -0.3% YoY, Q1 FY27 sequential -1.2%, Q2 FY27 guided flat-to-negative), while TCS's sequential cc growth this quarter (+0.4%) was still positive where Wipro's was negative — the tier-1 growth gap that has dogged Wipro for years has not closed. Quant screen concurs: quality_score 20.0 and growth_3y_score 12.5 are both weak, value_score 100 (statistically cheapest quintile) is a classic value-trap signature, and the systematic model already flags Reduce on both the 1y and 3y horizons (composite_3y 35.0, composite_1y 32.4). [DATA/INFERENCE]
recommendation_rationale: The bull case rests entirely on record deal bookings converting and on capital-return support; neither is a forward catalyst right now — the buyback is already done, and Wipro's own multi-year track record is that large TCV does not reliably convert into cc growth on the timeline management implies (Q1 FY27's own sequential revenue fell even as TCV rose). With Americas (60%+ of revenue) shrinking sequentially, margin compressing on wage/AI/H-1B costs, leadership churn mid-reorganization, and a valuation that already prices in only a ~5% growth bar Wipro has failed to clear for two straight years, there is no genuine evidence of an operating inflection — only promises of one. This is a name where the balance sheet is genuinely strong (low debt, high ROE/ROCE, well-funded payouts) but the operating business is not compounding, which argues for Sell over Hold: Hold would imply the growth/margin trajectory is merely pausing before resuming, and the data here does not support that yet.
summary: Wipro's June-quarter results (Q1 FY27) showed record large-deal bookings but revenue actually shrank versus the prior quarter, and margins fell further on wage hikes, deal ramp-up costs and the new US visa-fee headwind. Its largest market, the Americas, contracted again. The company just finished returning over $3 billion to shareholders via buyback and dividends — which is real and welcome — but that is now behind it, not ahead of it, and management's own guidance for the current quarter is flat to slightly down. The stock is fairly priced versus its own history and peers, not expensive, but it has not yet shown the growth needed to justify holding for upside from here.
positive_para: Wipro ended FY26 with record large-deal bookings ($16.4bn, +14% YoY) and Q1 FY27 large-deal TCV rose a further 12.9% sequentially to $1.63bn — genuine pipeline strength that, if it converts, supports better growth in FY28. The balance sheet is excellent (debt/equity 0.23, interest coverage 12.2x, ROE 15%, ROCE 18%), capital return has been substantial and disciplined (Rs 15,000cr buyback completed plus ongoing dividends, over $3bn returned in the trailing year), and the valuation at ~14x earnings is not demanding versus TCS/Infosys and at a clear discount to HCLTech. Management has also brought in fresh, credentialed leadership for the chronically weak consulting/Capco arm (an ex-Accenture executive reporting directly to the CEO), which is a real attempt to fix a known structural drag.
negative_para: The core problem has not changed: IT services revenue fell 0.3% YoY in FY26 and was down 1.2% sequentially in Q1 FY27, with Q2 FY27 guidance of -1.5% to +0.5% cc still flat-to-negative at the midpoint — two-plus years without organic growth despite record deal announcements each quarter. The Americas, 60%+ of revenue, contracted sequentially in both sub-segments this quarter, and Energy/Manufacturing/Resources fell 8.9% YoY. Margins compressed 130bps sequentially to 16.0% on wage hikes, ramp costs and AI investment, with the new $100k H-1B fee adding an industry-wide 50-150bps of further pressure into FY27. Leadership churn (Americas2 CEO resignation, CTO departure, a reorganized dual-CHRO structure) adds execution uncertainty exactly when consistent delivery is needed, and zero fresher hiring plus rising attrition (13.9%) both read as a company managing costs defensively, not gearing up for a growth cycle.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~14.1-14.2x trailing earnings — in line with TCS/Infosys and below HCLTech/sector average (~19x) — the market is pricing in only a modest, mid-single-digit (~5%) forward growth expectation, not a demanding one. The problem is Wipro has failed to clear even that modest bar for two consecutive fiscal years (FY26 IT services revenue -0.3% YoY; Q1 FY27 sequential -1.2%; Q2 FY27 guided flat-to-negative), despite record deal bookings each period. The multiple is fair-to-cheap on paper (value_score 100 in the quant screen) but this reads as a value trap rather than mispricing: cheap because growth/quality are genuinely weak (growth_3y_score 12.5, quality_score 20.0), not because the market is missing something. Vs. TCS (sequential cc +0.4% this quarter, still positive) the tier-1 growth gap persists.
